scenes.narration: Two thousand five hundred and sixty-four dollars. That is the average gross profit AutoNation, one of America's largest dealership groups, made on each new car it sold in twenty twenty-five. On a car that sold for about fifty-two thousand dollars.

Now the surprise. On the same deal, a small office at the back of the showroom made even more. The finance office earned two thousand seven hundred and sixty-nine dollars per car. More than the car itself.
So if the shiny car in the window is not where the money is, how does a car dealership really make its money?
By the end of this video, you will know the four engines of a dealership. The showroom, the finance office, the service bay, and the state laws that protect the whole business.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the size of the industry. According to the National Automobile Dealers Association, the country's sixteen thousand nine hundred and ninety franchised new-car dealers sold sixteen point two million vehicles in twenty twenty-five. Their total sales topped one point three trillion dollars. The average dealership sold about nine hundred and fifty-five new vehicles in the year, at an average retail price of about forty-eight thousand two hundred dollars. On paper, it looks like a business of selling cars.

And cars are expensive. Kelley Blue Book says the average new vehicle sold in September twenty twenty-six went for fifty thousand five hundred and sixty-two dollars, just below the all-time record. Carmakers were also spending an average of about three thousand three hundred and fifty-nine dollars per vehicle on incentives to keep cars moving. With prices like that, you would expect the dealer to keep a big slice.

It does not. At AutoNation, new vehicles brought in forty-nine percent of all revenue in twenty twenty-five, but only thirteen percent of gross profit. By our calculation, the gross margin on a new car was less than five percent. And it has been shrinking. Gross profit per new car fell from four thousand three hundred and forty-two dollars in twenty twenty-three to two thousand five hundred and sixty-four dollars in twenty twenty-five, and to two thousand one hundred and seventy-six in the third quarter of twenty twenty-six.

scenes.narration: Used cars are not much better. They made up twenty-eight percent of AutoNation's revenue, but only nine percent of its gross profit, about one thousand five hundred and fifty-five dollars per used car. Many of them arrive as trade-ins, which gives the dealer a second chance to profit from the same customer.

Let me draw the pie. Here is AutoNation's revenue, and almost half of it is new cars. Now here is its gross profit. The new-car slice shrinks to a sliver. The big pieces are somewhere else, in two places most buyers barely notice.

scenes.narration: The first is a small room you visit after you have already chosen your car. The finance office.

keyframes.label: After you choose your car…

scenes.narration: Most people do not pay cash for a car. They take a loan, often arranged right there at the dealership. The dealer does not lend the money itself. It places the loan with a bank or finance company, and earns a commission for it. It also sells extended warranties, service contracts and other protection products, again on commission.

Here is one way the commission can work. The lender sets a rate, called the buy rate. The dealer can offer you a higher rate, and the lender shares the difference with the dealer. That was described in a twenty thirteen bulletin from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which Congress later overturned. The Bureau's own advice is simple. Rates through dealers are often higher, and interest rates are negotiable.

Then come the add-ons. Gap insurance, extended warranties, paint protection. The CFPB notes that the cost of these products is often rolled into the loan amount. So you pay interest on them too, for years.

Add it up, and the finance office is a gold mine. At AutoNation, finance and insurance made up just five percent of revenue, but thirty percent of gross profit, one point four six billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. By our calculation, that is more than twice the gross profit it made selling new cars.

scenes.narration: Regulators tried to step in. In December twenty twenty-three, the Federal Trade Commission adopted the CARS Rule, banning charges for add-ons that give the buyer no benefit, and requiring dealers to get the buyer's express, informed consent for every charge. It expected to save consumers more than three point four billion dollars a year. The dealers' association sued. In January twenty twenty-five, a federal appeals court vacated the rule.

Let me draw the loan. Here is the price of the car. Add the add-ons, rolled into the loan. Add a slightly higher interest rate. Stretch it over almost six years. The monthly payment looks manageable, but the total paid grows, and part of that growth goes back to the dealer.

scenes.narration: But the most reliable money comes later, every time your car needs an oil change.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: According to NADA, America's franchised dealers wrote more than two hundred and seventy-six million repair orders in twenty twenty-five. Service and parts sales exceeded one hundred and sixty-four billion dollars. The average customer labor rate was one hundred and eighty-six dollars an hour.

At AutoNation, parts and service made up seventeen percent of revenue, but forty-eight percent of gross profit, the biggest share of all. By our calculation, almost half of every service dollar was gross profit. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, its share passed fifty-one percent.

And it is steady. In AutoNation's own words, parts and service has historically been less sensitive to the economy than selling cars. People can delay buying a new car. They cannot delay fixing the brakes. Warranty repairs are paid by the carmaker, so even a brand new car brings work back to the dealer.

Let me draw the life of one customer. Day one, the sale, a small profit. The same day, the loan and the warranty, a bigger one. Then, for years, oil changes, tires, brakes and repairs. The car is sold once. The customer is served again and again.

scenes.narration: Which raises a question. Why can carmakers not just sell directly to you and keep all that? The answer is in the law.

keyframes.label: Why can't carmakers sell to you?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In many states, franchise laws stand between the carmaker and the buyer. Michigan's law, for example, says a manufacturer may not sell a new car directly to a retail customer other than through franchised dealers.

These laws do more. A carmaker cannot simply end a dealer's franchise unless there is good cause. And a new dealer of the same brand often cannot open nearby. As AutoNation's annual report puts it, these franchise laws were designed to protect dealers.

Not everyone agrees with them. Staff at the Federal Trade Commission wrote in twenty fifteen that blanket bans on direct sales are an anomaly within the larger economy. Some newer electric carmakers have fought these rules state by state. But for most brands, the dealer remains the only door to the customer.

Let me draw the wall. Here is the carmaker. Here is you. Between you, a wall built by state law, with one door. The dealer stands in that door, and every sale, every loan and every repair passes through it.

scenes.narration: And on the other side of that door, the bill lands on the buyer.

scenes.narration: Americans now owe one point seven one trillion dollars on auto loans, according to the New York Fed. The Federal Reserve reports that the average rate on a seventy-two month new-car loan at commercial banks was seven point one seven percent in August twenty twenty-six.

Experian data published by NADA put the average monthly payment on a new car at about seven hundred and sixty-seven dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five, with an average term of almost sixty-nine months. That is close to six years of payments. And every extra month on the loan means more interest paid, and more years before the car is truly yours.

scenes.narration: And more buyers are struggling. The New York Fed says new delinquencies on auto loans remain at elevated levels. In the second quarter of twenty twenty-six, about three percent of auto loan balances moved into serious delinquency on an annual basis.

Let me put the dealership together. A thin profit on the car. A thick profit on the loan and the add-ons. A steady profit on every repair for years. And a law that keeps the door in the dealer's hands. The car is the bait. The customer is the business.

scenes.narration: So how do car dealerships really make money? Not mainly on the car you drive away in. On the loan you sign for it, the warranty you add to it, and the service bay you return to. Knowing that changes how you buy. Negotiate the price, but also the rate, the add-ons and the term. That is where the dealer's money really is.
